items.title: ‘Africa is being short-changed because we fail to negotiate well’ – Col Festus Aboagye
items.description: Retired Colonel Festus Aboagye has criticised African governments for failing to turn the continent’s vast natural and human resources into bargaining power, arguing that Africa is often short-changed because of weaknesses in its own negotiations. Speaking at the Students and Young Professionals Africa Liberty Academy (SYPALA) 2026 at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), organised by IMANI Africa on Thursday, August 27, Col. (Rtd) Aboagye said having abundant resources does not automatically give African countries influence in their dealings with foreign partners. “Having resources is not the same as controlling the value those resources create,” he said. The programme, organised in collaboration with IMANI Africa and UPSA, was held under the theme “Africa’s Future: Leadership in a Changing World”. According to Col. (Rtd) Aboagye, Africa continues to export much of its raw materials while capturing only a fraction of the value generated from finished products. He cited gold, oil and cocoa as examples, arguing that the continent has struggled to build the capacity needed to process its resources and retain more of the economic value. “We produce much of the raw material, but capture only a small share of the final product’s value,” he said. He said the same challenge applies to Africa’s large youth population, warning that demographic strength should not automatically be treated as an economic advantage. “Our young population is not automatically a dividend,” he said, citing the migration of Ghanaian nurses to other countries as an example of how African countries can invest in human capital only for other economies to benefit from it. For Col. (Rtd) Aboagye, the critical issue is therefore not simply whether Africa possesses valuable resources but whether governments can negotiate agreements that ensure those resources serve the continent’s long-term interests. “The real question is whether we can convert these numerous assets or diverse assets into leverage,” he said. He urged African governments to pay greater attention to the terms of agreements they sign with foreign partners. “The decisive variable is not a partner. It is the terms,” he said. “What are the terms that you are going to write when they want access to any of your resources?” Col. (Rtd) Aboagye used Ghana’s dealings with Turkey over a power plant as an example of what he described as weaknesses in negotiating capacity. He said Turkey brought the technology needed for the project, while Ghana had the resources required to operate it, but questioned whether Ghana secured the best possible terms. “When we needed technology in the form of the power plant that Turkey was providing, they had the technology. We have the oil or whatever to put in there in order to address our needs. But what did we write on that paper? What did we sign to?” he asked. He further cited the involvement of the Africa Centre for Energy Policy (ACEP), saying the organisation was brought in to help renegotiate the deal and succeeded in reducing its cost. That example, he said, demonstrated the importance of independent expertise when governments negotiate major agreements. Col. (Rtd) Aboagye rejected the idea that Africa’s economic challenges can be blamed entirely on foreign partners. “Africa is being short-changed, not because our partners are short-changing us, but because we ourselves as Africans,” he said. He argued that African governments must develop stronger negotiating institutions and become more deliberate about what they seek from international partnerships. He also urged governments to consult independent organisations with technical expertise before concluding major agreements. “We refuse to consult institutions like IMANI and ACEP and CDD, CODEO, and all of these organisations which have the expertise,” he said. He said the problem is compounded when political leaders approach negotiations with considerations that are narrower than the national interest. “For everybody in government who is negotiating an agreement… there’s a term, what is in need for us?” he said. According to him, political actors can sometimes focus on what their party or individual officeholders stand to gain instead of asking what will benefit Ghana in the long term. “What can the party get? What can you, as the minister, get? You see what I mean? Not what can Ghana get,” he said. The retired military officer also argued that Africa has an opportunity to improve its bargaining position because several major powers are competing for access to the continent’s resources, markets and strategic influence. He listed China, the United States, the European Union, Russia, the Gulf States, India, Turkey and Brazil among the external actors seeking partnerships with African countries. “They are here because they have interests that they think Africa can satisfy for them,” he said. He explained that foreign partners offer different combinations of capital, technology, security, markets and infrastructure, while seeking access, influence, resources or political support in return. The challenge, he said, is for African countries to understand these interests and negotiate from a position that maximises their own benefits. “The fact that we have six youths looking for these things means that we can sit in our rooms and see how we can maximise these things that they are looking for, to our benefit,” he said. He advocated a strategy of multi-alignment, where African countries avoid becoming permanently tied to one global power and instead choose partnerships based on their strategic interests. “That will depend on, first of all, the capacity that you have to negotiate,” he said. He identified negotiating capacity, fiscal independence and domestic legitimacy as important factors that determine whether African countries can exercise meaningful strategic choice. Col. (Rtd) Aboagye also cautioned against confusing Africa’s growing strategic importance with actual geopolitical power. “Africa is being courted. And that is better than being ignored,” he said. “But being wanted is not the same as being strong.” He said Africa’s 54 votes at international institutions could constitute significant influence if countries were able to coordinate their positions around common strategic interests. “54 votes cast together are a source of influence. But 54 votes cast separately are not opportunities,” he said. He also pointed to Africa’s limited influence in the United Nations Security Council, noting that despite longstanding efforts to reform the global system, the continent has not secured a permanent seat with veto power. He said the continent must therefore focus not only on being heard internationally but also on developing the capacity to act collectively and protect its interests. “Being heard is not the same as being able to act,” he said.

items.title: NSMQ 2026: PRESEC Legon keeps 9th title dream alive as Mfantsipim looms in quarter-finals
items.description: PRESEC, Legon, have survived their first major test of the 2026 National Science and Maths Quiz (NSMQ), powering past St. Louis SHS and Islamic SHS, Kumasi to keep their record-extending title hopes alive. The eight-time champions seized control from the opening round, leading 23–17–8 before extending their advantage to 40 points in Round Two. PRESEC then turned up the heat in the Problem of the Day, picking up 8 of the available 10 points to reach 48 points. St. Louis fought back in Round Four and had their own perfect moment, answering all True or False questions correctly to secure the Jupay Clean Sheet. But that could not derail PRESEC, who still stretched their lead to 58 points and eventually finished on 67 points. St. Louis ended on 47 points, with Islamic SHS on 19 points. Now comes the real test. The defending champions have already dispatched Wesley Girls and are waiting in the quarterfinals. Having won the competition in 2024 and 2025, Mfantsipim are chasing a historic third consecutive title and their fifth overall. PRESEC, however, are hunting for number nine. With eight national titles already in the cabinet, the record champions will now face the school standing between them and another step towards history. items.title: La SOMELEC annonce le retour à la normale des postes de transformation électriques Est et Nord
items.description: La Société mauritanienne d’électricité « Somelec » a annoncé le retour à la normale des deux postes de transformation électrique de l’Est et du Nord, situés respectivement à Toujounine et à Tevrag Zeina. Le directeur général de la société, Kharambale Lehbib, a déclaré que les travaux de réparation effectués avaient permis de remettre les deux postes en service à 100 %. Il a ajouté, dans une déclaration rapportée par l’Agence mauritanienne d’information (AMI), que les travaux de réparation visant à remettre en service à 100 % la sous-station se sont achevés. Les deux transformateurs fonctionnent correctement à ce jour, et tous les quartiers raccordés à cette sous-station sont alimentés en électricité, à savoir les zones de Toujounine, Dar Naïm, Tarhil et Mellah. Il a souligné que le défi consiste désormais à garantir le fonctionnement continu de ces équipements dans de telles conditions, un défi que nous relèverons au cours des jours et des semaines à venir, selon ses propres termes. Cette centrale a été remise en état de fonctionnement normal grâce à la remise en service des cellules de 15 kV, après leur réparation et leur mise en service, ainsi qu’au recours à des équipements de secours dont disposait la société, en plus de l’importation d’autres équipements de l’étranger.

items.title: Zoomlion begins fumigation exercise across Eastern Region after floods
items.description: Zoomlion Ghana Limited has begun a disinfestation and fumigation exercise across all 33 Municipal and District Assemblies in the Eastern Region to help prevent disease outbreaks following recent floods. The exercise, which started on Friday, August 21, is expected to end on September 30. It is being carried out by Zoomlion’s Vector Control Unit in collaboration with the assemblies as part of the company’s corporate social responsibility programme. The exercise targets markets, lorry parks, public toilets, refuse container sites and other areas that could harbour disease-causing organisms, particularly during the rainy season. The intervention is aimed at controlling disease vectors and reducing the risk of cholera, malaria, typhoid and other infections, especially in flood-affected communities. Briefing the media at Agartha Market in Koforidua to officially launch the exercise, Eastern Regional Manager of Zoomlion, Cynthia Gbadago, said the initiative was prompted by the extent of flooding recorded across the country, particularly in the Eastern Region. She said the floods had left some areas contaminated, making the exercise necessary to protect residents from potential disease outbreaks. Mrs Gbadago said Zoomlion had already educated market women and residents on the exercise and urged them to cover food and drinking water before fumigation. She advised residents to wait between four and six hours before re-entering areas that had been fumigated. She also urged residents to protect their environment by disposing of refuse properly and avoiding indiscriminate dumping, which she said could contribute to disease outbreaks. The Eastern Regional Environmental Officer, Prince Osei Kissi, commended Zoomlion for its support and partnership with the assemblies. He assured residents that his outfit would continue to work with the company to ensure the exercise is carried out effectively across the region. Traders welcome exercise At the Agartha Market, trader Georgina Agbesi expressed hope that the exercise would eliminate harmful insects, including mosquitoes and cockroaches, as well as rodents such as mice. Another trader, Afia Adutwumwaa, appealed to the government to provide adequate public toilet facilities and address recurring flooding at the market during heavy rains. Both traders expressed appreciation to Zoomlion and the assemblies for the intervention.

items.title: A ‘Boring’ Democrat the Party Wants to Emulate
items.description: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture. Sign up for it here. Last summer, North Carolina’s race for U.S. Senate was expected to be among the most exciting in the 2026 cycle. Thom Tillis, a Republican, had opted not to run for reelection. Donald Trump had recruited Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee, to stand in his place. Roy Cooper, a former two-term governor, seemed like Democrats’ best and only hope to make the race competitive in a state Trump had won three times—and where no Democrat has won a Senate race since 2008. Today, other contests are attracting more attention, and North Carolina has been a bit of a snooze. It hasn’t yet been the billion-dollar election some observers predicted. Whatley, a first-time candidate, has struggled to gain traction, and Cooper has gone from last hope to strong favorite. Cooper’s team isn’t declaring victory yet. “This is going to be a two-to-three-point race at the end of the day,” his longtime strategist, Morgan Jackson, told me. “We know that it’s a 50–50 state and you win or lose on the margins.” But most forecasters rate the race as leaning toward a Cooper win. As the Democratic Party struggles to define its identity in the Trump era, Cooper’s purple-state success has drawn lots of attention. National press coverage has hailed Cooper’s campaign as “boring” (complimentary) and “ normal .” That lack of intrigue comes as a relief to a party dealing with drama and outrage in many other races. Cooper hasn’t taken controversial political stands like Michigan’s Abdul el-Sayed has, and he doesn’t have the personal scandals of the erstwhile Maine candidate Graham Platner. Republican voters also haven’t found ways to call him weird like they have Texas’s James Talarico. It’s natural for Democrats to want to emulate Cooper’s success, but I’m skeptical that he offers any simple, transportable lessons. That isn’t to say that descriptions such as boring and normal are wrong. When I asked Jackson point-blank whether Cooper was boring, he didn’t exactly dispute the notion. “He’s a workhorse; he’s not a show horse,” he said. “He’s a steady hand. So voters don’t see him out there as a lightning rod.” Cooper’s first big asset is that he has a long relationship with North Carolina voters. He entered statewide elected office in the waning days of the Bill Clinton presidency, a stretch that ended only in January 2025, after two terms as governor. This means that any Republican candidate will struggle to define Cooper in their own terms. This longevity is also a product of Cooper’s cautiousness. Almost from the moment he became attorney general in 2001, he was expected to someday run for senator or governor. But he didn’t actually do so until 2016, when he eked out a win over incumbent Republican Governor Pat McCrory by a little more than 10,000 votes. He waited to jump into the Senate race until shortly after Tillis’s retirement announcement, which meant that he was likely able to scare off Republicans more formidable than Whatley. He also picked an extremely favorable cycle for Democrats nationally. Cooper’s caution and affability shouldn’t be taken for softness. Chris Cooper, a political scientist at Western Carolina University (of no relation to the candidate), sometimes jokes that Roy Cooper is like Mister Rogers , if Mister Rogers carried a switchblade. Andrew Dunn, a North Carolina writer and Republican operative, is less complimentary . “Roy Cooper has carefully cultivated a public persona as your friendly, easygoing grandpa who wears sweaters and talks quietly,” he told me. “That is far from his private persona. He is incredibly opportunistic and calculating.” As governor, Cooper used a range of tricks to promote his agenda. He waged a war of attrition against the Republicans who controlled the state legislature over Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act. GOP leaders started out dead set against it; Cooper finally got the expansion passed in 2023, his penultimate year in office. He also wielded his veto more frequently than any past governor. (North Carolina was the last state in the union to give its governor veto power, doing so in 1997 via legislation championed by a young state senator named Roy Cooper.) After Republicans overrode some of Cooper’s vetoes, he led a push to break their supermajority and backed a successful primary challenge to a Democratic lawmaker who’d sometimes voted with the GOP . When Cooper was replaced in 2025 by his fellow Democrat Josh Stein, Raleigh Republicans professed relief at being able to deal with someone they viewed as more agreeable (or, a cynic might say, whom they thought they could more easily outflank).​​ Contending with a unified Republican general assembly constrained Cooper on policy, but it may also have benefited him politically. Because Democrats have spent the past 15 years desperately trying to stave off conservative legislation, the party has had little room for internecine warfare. As a result, Cooper has sidestepped the kinds of battles that might have gotten him pigeonholed as a liberal or a moderate. (The only Republican governor in that stretch, meanwhile, lasted only one term, sunk in part by battles with GOP lawmakers.) Some conservatives also feel that Cooper gets a free pass from the press. This summer, Whatley’s campaign barred journalists from mainstream and left-leaning outlets from events, while Cooper’s campaign turned away staffers from two conservative outlets, but local coverage focused more heavily on Whatley. Dunn told me he still believes that Whatley could win. He takes some hope from a 1984 race, when popular former two-term Democratic Governor Jim Hunt ran against Senator Jesse Helms. “Helms spent millions upon millions of dollars trying to convince North Carolinians that they didn’t really like Governor Hunt’s record as governor,” Dunn said. “It didn’t work.” Early polls showed Hunt well ahead, but in the last phase of the campaign, Helms emphasized national issues and won. To do something like this, Dunn contends , Whatley could argue that Cooper will be another vote for the Democratic agenda, no matter how nice people think he is. But Helms also benefited from President Ronald Reagan’s landslide victory in 1984; Whatley is a close ally of Trump, who is both not on the ballot and sinking in popularity. Jackson told me he believes that voters’ opinions of Cooper are already set anyway. “People see him as a genuine guy,” he said. “The reality is, Roy Cooper is as authentic as they come.” One argument for his authenticity might be how hard he is for Democrats to replicate elsewhere. Related: The Democrats’ biggest Senate recruits have one thing in common. What North Carolina and Roy Cooper can teach Democrats (From 2021) Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : Peter Wehner on the wrath of MAGA Spencer Cox’s possibly delusional crusade Americans are spending luxury dollars for dive-bar service. Today’s News More than 350 people have been killed and more than 1,300 remain missing after flash floods struck Nepal and China yesterday. The U.S. Geological Survey said that a glacial collapse and resulting debris flow triggered the flooding; Chinese authorities warned that a dam created by the landslide could breach and cause further flooding. Jurors began deliberating in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy , who killed her three young children at their Massachusetts home in 2023. Clancy is charged with first-degree murder; her defense argues that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis. President Trump signed an executive order directing the U.S. government to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” The move comes amid escalating tensions between the United States and Canada following the breakdown of trade talks and the addition of new tariffs. Dispatches Time-Travel Thursdays : For centuries, some have lamented the erosion of the South’s distinctive approach to etiquette , Annie Joy Williams writes. Work in Progress : Rogé Karma on why data centers are a distraction . Explore all of our newsletters here. Evening Read Joe Raedle / Getty Not American Enough By Toluse Olorunnipa For Carlos Alemán, the pinnacle of the dozen years since he became a U.S. citizen was the night in 2020 when he was elected to serve on the city council of Homewood, Alabama. One of the lowest moments came earlier this year, when he learned that some of the most powerful people in his state are attempting to ban immigrants like him from pursuing higher office. “It seems to be part of a project to reject anyone who’s not born in this country as not worthy or deserving of the full rights of citizenship,” Alemán, who was born in Nicaragua, told me. For most of American history, becoming a citizen has meant acquiring the right to participate in virtually all aspects of civic life, including voting, serving on juries, and mounting a campaign for any political office other than the presidency. But in Alabama and other states across the country, Republican lawmakers are now pushing to make an important distinction: Naturalized citizens, they argue, should not have the same right to serve in public office as someone born in the United States. Read the full article. More From The Atlantic Duncan Hosie: The Supreme Court isn’t interested in facts. But their relationship—and Avery’s influence— was more complicated than that , Sebastian Smee argues. Reminisce. items.title: Migration clandestine : 161 personnes secourues par les garde-côtes mauritaniens dans la wilaya de l’Inchiri
items.description: La garde côtière mauritanienne a annoncé avoir secouru 161 personnes qui se trouvaient à bord d'un bateau d'immigration clandestine, au large de la région de M’Heïjratt, dans la wilaya de l'Inchiri, après l'avoir repéré dans les eaux relevant de la souveraineté mauritanienne. Dans un communiqué, la garde côtière a indiqué que l’embarcation avait pris la mer depuis la capitale gambienne, Banjul, et était restée en mer pendant environ huit jours avant que ses unités n’interviennent et ne parviennent à secourir toutes les personnes qui se trouvaient à son bord. Selon les données communiquées, la plupart des personnes secourues sont de nationalité sénégalaise ; elles sont au nombre de 99, dont 91 hommes, 6 femmes et 2 enfants. On dénombre par ailleurs 56 Guinéens, dont 3 hommes, 38 femmes et 15 enfants, ainsi que 6 Gambiens, dont 2 hommes et 4 femmes.

items.title: Police suspend concrete mixer truck operations in Accra and Tema for 3 days
items.description: The Ghana Police Service has announced a three-day suspension of operations by concrete mixer trucks in Accra and Tema following concerns over concrete spillages, road safety and damage to road infrastructure. The restriction will take effect from Friday, 28 August, to Sunday, 30 August 2026, the Ghana Police Service said in a statement issued on Thursday. The decision was announced after the police, under the auspices of the National Security Secretariat, engaged owners and operators of transit mixer trucks, also known as concrete mixer trucks, to discuss road safety and compliance with road traffic regulations. The meeting was led by the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), Mr Christian Tetteh Yohuno, and brought together key stakeholders to address concerns surrounding the operation of the trucks and their impact on other road users and public infrastructure. According to the police, stakeholders raised concerns about the spillage of concrete and other materials from the trucks while they are being transported or operated on the roads. Such spillages, the police said, can obstruct traffic, create hazards for motorists and other road users, and damage road surfaces. Operators were therefore urged to take steps to ensure that concrete and other materials are not discharged or left on public roads during transportation and operations. As part of measures to address the problem, concrete mixer truck operators were served notice that they would not be permitted to operate on roads within Accra and Tema from Friday to Sunday. The police said the temporary restriction is intended to allow authorities to clear and clean road surfaces affected by concrete and other materials. “During the suspension period, concrete mixer trucks are not to undertake delivery operations within Accra,” the police said. The directive applies to vehicles operating in the affected areas during the three-day period. The police warned that any vehicle found moving in breach of the directive would face enforcement action. “Any vehicle found moving in breach of the directive will be subject to appropriate enforcement action in accordance with the law,” the statement said. The engagement formed part of efforts by the security authorities to improve compliance with road traffic regulations and address problems linked to the use of heavy commercial vehicles on the country’s roads. Representatives from the Ministry of Roads and Highways and the Ghana Highways Authority were present at the meeting, alongside owners and operators of concrete mixer trucks. Concrete mixer trucks are commonly used to transport freshly mixed concrete to construction sites. Because of the nature of their operations, spillages can leave concrete deposits on roads, creating potential dangers for vehicles and pedestrians and making affected sections of road difficult to use.

items.title: The Generational Difference in Southern Manners
items.description: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present. Sign up here. It is a truth universally acknowledged that the southerner is the most mannerly person in America. Before any Yanks get defensive, I want to clarify that this does not necessarily make them the kindest group in America. As a young child in Tennessee, I learned that a “Bless your heart” to one’s face paired particularly well with a cutting remark behind closed doors. I also learned that etiquette was a pesky but persistent thing: Anytime I replied to my father with a curt “yes,” he’d look at me sideways and say, “Yes, what?” I’d sigh. “Yes sir .” My father is a seventh-generation Kentuckian, and my mother’s family has lived in the South since the 18th century. Growing up, I knew that there was a regalia to the southerner’s manners that might come as a surprise to those who cast the region as unrefined. Men are to hold doors for their dates and give up their seats to women on the bus. In some spaces, they will still stand when a lady enters or exits the room. There are also the more casual types of manners. When you pass any stranger on the street, you say, “Howdy,” or, “How are you?” You wave at pedestrians you drive by in your truck. You let neighbors borrow an egg or a cup of sugar without any expectation of repayment. Even as the identity of the South evolves, and more young people lose certain traits that are identifiably southern , manners remain one of the region’s most distinctive and steadfast qualities. The region’s attitudes toward hospitality are a natural outgrowth of these broader social graces. In the South, people like to emphasize that anyone’s cousin’s neighbor’s friend will be welcome in your home. As Walter H. Page described in The Atlantic in 1881, if a stranger comes “with a letter of introduction from some of their old friends, or if he happen to be connected, however distantly, with an old family known to them, he will at once be taken into their homes, and he will receive every hospitality.” This kindness has its limits, however. “The South is famous for its courtesy, but the highly refined concept of honor that largely produced its manners has also helped to make the region the most violent in the country,” Benjamin Schwarz noted in a 1997 Atlantic essay. “A s the old saying goes, a southerner is gracious and friendly until he is mad enough to kill you.” Although plenty of southerners are motivated to adhere to codes of etiquette by a sense of selflessness and responsibility, the manners that they are so careful to keep are also an effort to protect their reputation. And a well-mannered person isn’t necessarily a mild-mannered person. One 1996 study compared the behaviors of white male University of Michigan students who grew up in the North with those who grew up in the South: When a man bumped into a student and called him an asshole, the students raised in the South were more likely to think that their masculine reputation was threatened and respond aggressively. You also cannot tell the story of southern manners without telling the story of Black southerners—specifically, the story of their enslavement and its lingering effects. “A Southerner of the upper class delighted in saying that he was taught his manners by his ‘Black Mammy,’” Jessie W. Parkhurst, the then-dean of women at the Tuskegee Institute, wrote in 1938. Many enslaved women who worked domestic roles were made to care for white children. Beginning in the antebellum era, they were caricatured as grateful and devoted caregivers, even as they were being underpaid and overworked. Long after the abolition of slavery, many white southerners, including my father, who was born into the first breaths of the civil-rights movement, were still raised by Black nannies. (This is true outside the South as well—the majority of domestic workers in America today are women of color.) My father, like many other white southerners, learned most of his manners from the nanny with whom he spent so many hours of his childhood. The courtesies shown in the region have long been “the product of the fusion of black and white attitudes,” Schwarz noted in his essay . But politeness was often forced on Black southerners because their lives depended on it: As recently as decades ago, any perceived violations of etiquette, including simply making eye contact with white people, could provoke brutal beatings and lynchings. And Black contributions to manners were rarely given equal import. After slavery was outlawed, Black women had limited employment prospects in the Jim Crow era and the years after, and they were usually severely underpaid. Today, the extent to which southerners are mannerly has evolved, as all things do. Some southerners lament what they see as a recent loss to their distinctive approach to etiquette, but this was already the case in 1897, when W. P. Trent wrote in this magazine , “We have seen that the Southerner’s basis of character is a fine one, and that he is becoming, year by year, more thoroughly nationalized.” He explained that “external manners have undoubtedly changed: there is now less suavity, less punctiliousness, less attention to small details, than of old; but this was true of the South of 1860 as compared with that of 1760, and means nothing but progress in the direction of greater freedom and individuality in conformity with the rest of the world.” Part of the reason could be that more people are moving to the South. In January, I wrote about the disappearing southern drawl , another aspect of the region’s culture that is noticeably changing. I noted that, according to the U.S. census, the South gained more residents than all other regions combined from 2023 to 2024. I also found that the proliferation of the internet has undeniably altered southern culture; young kids are exposed to different behaviors on social media, and their role models aren’t just nannies or teachers or parents—they now come in the form of content creators and online friends. These factors may be driving the shift in southern manners writ large. I’ve observed a generational difference even in my own family. My sisters still live in Tennessee, and I live in New York City, but none of us spends our days quite like our mother. She will make warm conversation with strangers whenever she possibly can. Living in a big city can often hurry me out of this habit. She’ll fill your plate a second or third time despite your saying you couldn’t possibly have another bite. I offer my guests a glass of wine and whatever nonperishable snack they can scavenge from the pantry. She will listen to a story she has heard hundreds of times with the enthusiasm of it being its first telling. My sisters and I don’t have this same patience. But time spent with my mother, who puts hours of care and kindness into daily interactions, always reminds me of the goodness to be found in doing the mannerly thing—in being inquisitive, leaving a kind note, shouting “How are ya?” at the neighbor, knowing that it may turn into a two-hour conversation. Sometimes these niceties are more than just nice. In an age of constant hurry, they’re also an excuse to slow down, if only for a moment.

Tuy/ Fin de l’immersion patriotique 2026 : plus de 500 jeunes bacheliers s’engagent à accompagner la dynamique de la Révolution progressiste populaire
items.description: Tuy/ Fin de l'immersion patriotique 2026 : plus de 500 jeunes bacheliers s’engagent à accompagner la dynamique de la Révolution progressiste populaire Houndé, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – La cérémonie de clôture de l’Immersion patriotique obligatoire (IPO) 2026 dans la province du Tuy s’est tenue, ce jeudi au stade Kiéni de Houndé, sous la présidence du Haut-commissaire de la province, Issiaka Segda. Elle marque la fin d’un mois d’immersion de plus de 500 jeunes bacheliers de la province. La cérémonie s’est déroulée en présence des autorités administratives, des responsables des services techniques, des encadreurs et animateurs, des formateurs ainsi que de nombreux parents. Les appelés ont présenté plusieurs démonstrations, notamment en ordre serré, en secourisme et en technique d’intervention opérationnelle rapprochée (TIOR), avant de clôturer la cérémonie par un défilé. La représentante des appelés de l’IPO 2026 du Tuy, Dabankiè Hortense Léticia Nioumou, a indiqué que cette immersion leur a permis de vivre une expérience humaine, éducative et patriotique enrichissante. « A travers cette immersion, nous avons mieux compris la vision portée par le Camarade Président du Faso, Chef de l’État, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré », a-t-elle déclaré. Elle a souligné que les appelés ont également appris des valeurs utiles dans leur vie quotidienne et leurs futures responsabilités, notamment le patriotisme, le civisme, l’ordre, la discipline, la solidarité, l’entraide, la cohésion sociale ainsi que le respect des autres et de la culture. Au nom de ses camarades, elle s’est engagée à mettre en pratique les enseignements reçus et à participer activement et avec responsabilité à la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP), afin de contribuer à bâtir un Burkina Faso souverain, résilient et prospère. Le Haut-commissaire Issiaka Segda, par ailleurs président de la cellule provinciale de l’IPO du Tuy, a invité les appelés à traduire dans leurs comportements quotidiens, leurs choix et leur engagement, les enseignements reçus au cours de l’immersion. Selon lui, cette deuxième édition revêt une importance particulière pour la province du Tuy, car elle s’est déroulée sur le territoire provincial. Il s’est réjoui de la capacité de la province à accueillir et à organiser une activité d’une telle importance et a salué l’ensemble des acteurs ayant contribué au bon déroulement de l’immersion. Le Haut-Commissaire a par ailleurs rappelé aux appelés que la fin de leur formation ne signifie pas la fin de leur engagement patriotique. « Faites de votre comportement quotidien le meilleur témoignage de cette immersion. Que vos familles soient fières de vous. Que votre province soit fière de vous et surtout que votre nation puisse compter sur vous », a-t-il conseillé. Agence d’Information du Burkina BEB/wis

items.title: Nando : les acteurs de l’excellence au primaire récompensés pour leurs performances
items.description: BURKINA-NANDO-EDUCATION-DREPPNF-EXCELLENCE-SCOLAIRE Nando : les acteurs de l’excellence au primaire récompensés pour leurs performances Koudougou, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – La Direction régionale de l’éducation préscolaire, primaire et non formelle (DREPPNF) de Nando a célébré le mercredi 26 août, sa Journée régionale de l’excellence au primaire au cours de laquelle les meilleurs acteurs ont été récompensés pour leurs performances. C'est sous le thème : « Promotion des langues nationales dans la région de Nando, gage de notre souveraineté culturelle », que l'excellence scolaire de cette année a été célébrée. La cérémonie, placée sous le patronage du ministre de l'enseignement de base, de l'alphabétisation et de la promotion des langues nationales, Jacques sosthène Dingara, le parrainage du Dr Jean Marie Vianney Yaméogo et de Bonsdawendé Alfred Yaméogo, a été marquée par la récompense des meilleurs acteurs de l’éducation. La célébration a réuni les autorités administratives, les responsables de l’éducation, les enseignants, les élèves, les parents d’élèves ainsi que plusieurs partenaires de l’éducation. L’un des temps forts de la cérémonie a été l’exécution de l’hymne national en langue mooré, suivie de la projection d’une capsule vidéo consacrée à la promotion des langues nationales. La particularité de cette journée réside également dans le fait que la plupart des interventions ont été prononcées en langue mooré, donnant ainsi une dimension concrète au thème de la cérémonie. Dans le message du ministre de l’Enseignement de base, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des langues nationales, lu par le représentant du gouverneur, le secrétaire général de la région de Nando, Lucien Guéguéré, le ministre a salué les performances réalisées par la région au Certificat d’études primaires (CEP), session 2026. Il a estimé que ces résultats contribuent à la promotion d’une culture de la qualité, indispensable à la transformation du système éducatif. Le ministre a également invité les acteurs de l’éducation à poursuivre la mise en œuvre des réformes, notamment la valorisation des langues nationales, considérées comme un socle de l’identité culturelle et un levier de souveraineté. Le directeur régional de l’éducation préscolaire, primaire et non formelle de Nando, Abylaicé Rouamba, s’est dit satisfait des résultats obtenus. « Tout travail mérite salaire, tout effort accompli mérite une reconnaissance », a-t-il déclaré, avant d’appeler les acteurs à redoubler d’efforts pour améliorer davantage les performances scolaires. La cérémonie a été l’occasion de distinguer les meilleurs enseignants et les meilleures Circonscriptions d’éducation de base (CEB). Les lauréats ont reçu divers prix, notamment des motos, des vélos, des ordinateurs, des tablettes, des lettres de félicitations ainsi que des enveloppes financières. Parmi les récipiendaires figure Edmond Bama, issu de la CEB de Didyr, école de Mogueya, distingué meilleur enseignant de la région, pour avoir fait un taux de 100% avec 119 élèves. Pour lui, cette reconnaissance est le fruit de plusieurs années de travail et d’engagement auprès des élèves. « Il faut aimer les enfants. Si tu n’as pas l’amour des enfants, tu ne peux pas avoir de résultats », a-t-il confié. Chez les élèves, Légma Nansi Richèle, de l’école de Ténado A, a obtenu 173,5 points au CEP. Heureuse de ses récompenses, notamment une tablette, un sac et un vélo, elle a expliqué que ces cadeaux lui permettront de mieux poursuivre ses études. Le camarade Yaméogo, conseiller des affaires économiques au ministère de l’Économie et des Finances, parrain de la cérémonie, a, pour sa part, exprimé sa fierté d’accompagner cette initiative. Il a salué les performances de Nando, qui avoisinent 93 % au CEP, et souhaité la pérennisation de cette dynamique d’excellence. Le secrétaire général de la région, Lucien Guéguéré, représentant le gouverneur, a rappelé que « un pays riche en ressources naturelles, sans ressources humaines de qualité, ne connaîtra pas de développement ». Il a ainsi encouragé la poursuite des efforts en faveur d’une éducation de qualité, véritable moteur du développement de la région et du Burkina Faso. Agence d'information du Burkina FGB/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: Parliament approves Mahama Ayariga and Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings as ministers
items.description: Parliament has approved the nominations of Mahama Ayariga as Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs and Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings as Minister for Environment, Science and Technology. The approval was given on Thursday evening, August 27, 2026, following their vetting earlier in the day by Parliament’s Appointments Committee. The House approved both nominations through a voice vote, with the Speaker declaring that the Ayes had it. Announcing the decision, the Speaker said the approval was in accordance with Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution. “Honourable Members, the Ayes have it. This Honourable House has accordingly approved the nominations of His Excellency the President of the following persons as Ministers of State in accordance with Article 78(1) of the 1992 Constitution,” he declared. The approval followed the consideration of the Appointments Committee’s report on the nominees after their vetting earlier in the day. During their respective appearances before the committee, the nominees responded to questions on their competence, policy priorities and plans for their respective ministries. Dr Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who is set to take charge of the Environment, Science and Technology portfolio, spoke extensively on Ghana’s approach to climate finance, plastic waste management and the role of science and technology in addressing environmental challenges. She called for greater investment in research and innovation, including support for the Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) to develop biodegradable alternatives to conventional plastics. She also advocated stronger measures to address landfill pollution, including the use of non-permeable bases to prevent leachate from contaminating soil and groundwater. Mr Mahama Ayariga, whose nomination was also approved, is expected to lead the Ministry of Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs. The approval clears the way for both nominees to be formally appointed and assume their respective ministerial responsibilities, subject to the completion of the remaining constitutional processes.

items.title: Lake Ontario: Carney rejects Trump’s renaming, says name will remain
items.description: By Favour Ulebor & Agency report Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday rejected United States President Donald Trump’s move to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”, insisting that the water body would continue to be known by its existing name. Carney said the name “Lake Ontario” was more than 400 years old and predated both the Confederation of Canada and the Declaration of Independence of the United States. In his X post, Carney noted, “The name is more than 400 years ​old, predating ​both the Confederation of Canada ‌and ⁠the Declaration of Independence of the United States of ​America. “Canadians also know that ​naming reality ​means ⁠calling it Lake Ontario – then, now ⁠and ​always.” The development came amid growing tensions between Canada and the United States over trade, following the collapse of negotiations between the two countries. Carney had on Tuesday announced that Canada would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of US goods from September 8, 2026. The decision followed the Trump administration’s imposition of 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods after trade negotiations between the two countries broke down. The failure of last-minute negotiations on Friday marked a fresh strain in the Canada-US relationship, which has for decades been regarded as one of the most integrated and stable bilateral partnerships. Data from the US Embassy shows that trade in goods and services between the two countries averages about $2.5 billion daily. Carney said Canada had recognised that “America has changed” and that the two countries would “not return to our old relationship.” Trump subsequently intensified the confrontation on Monday, telling Canadian leaders to “fall in line.” The United States buys between $380 billion and $400 billion worth of goods from Canada annually, accounting for about 12 to 14 per cent of total US imports. Canada also accounts for about 14 per cent of total US exports, making it one of the United States’ largest trading partners. However, the trade relationship remains heavily dependent on the US market, with Canada buying about 62.2 per cent of its imported goods from the US and sending about 72 per cent of its exports to the US. The tariffs affect several sectors, including steel, dairy products, appliances and paper. However, some highly integrated sectors, including crude oil and automobile manufacturing, have largely been excluded in a bid to prevent severe price increases and disruptions on both sides of the border. The latest measures are part of a wider series of retaliatory actions by countries, including China and the European Union, in response to US tariff policies. Trade experts, including Robert Lawrence, have described such measures as protectionist policies aimed at protecting domestic industries and increasing political leverage in international negotiations. The long-term impact of the escalating trade disputes between the United States and its trading partners remains uncertain. The post Lake Ontario: Carney rejects Trump’s renaming, says name will remain appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Le parti « la Mauritanie en avant » suspend sa participation aux préparatives du dialogue national avant la libération de l’un de ses dirigeants en détention
items.description: Le président du parti « La Mauritanie en avant », Nourredine Mohamedou, a déclaré que son parti suspendrait sa participation à toutes les activités préparatoires au dialogue national tant que ses dirigeants seraient en prison, à moins que des preuves tangibles d’un délit à leur encontre ne soient établies, ajoutant que le parti ne pouvait pas dialoguer avec les autorités dans ces circonstances. Noureddine a précisé, lors d’une intervention ce jeudi sur « Sahara 24 », que le dirigeant Lebatt Ould Mayouf avait été emmené de chez lui hier, jour de la fête de la naissance du Prophète, et qu’il se trouvait actuellement au bureau de la cybercriminalité relevant de l’état-major de la Gendarmerie nationale. Noureddine a indiqué que le parti ignorait, à ce jour, le mobile de cette arrestation et n’avait reçu aucune information la justifiant, les autorités n’en ayant pas non plus expliqué au parti ses motifs. Le président du parti « Mauritanie en avant », a demandé au président de la république la libération immédiate du dirigeant détenu, soulignant qu’il n’avait commis aucun délit et qu’il exerçait son droit légal et constitutionnel d’exprimer son opinion, selon ses propres termes. Évoquant un enregistrement audio circulant sur les réseaux sociaux et attribué au dirigeant, Nourredine a affirmé qu’il s’agissait d’un « enregistrement mensonger et fabriqué de toutes pièces. Selon lui la voix dans le vocal n’est pas celle de Lebatt Ould Mayouf », précisant qu’il s’agissait d’un faux dans lequel une voix enregistrée avait été superposée à l’image du dirigeant. Les autorités mauritaniennes avaient convoqué le membre du bureau exécutif du parti « La Mauritanie en avant », le général à la retraite Lebatt Ould Mayouf, et lui avaient demandé de se présenter devant le procureur de la République.

items.title: NACOC, University of Ghana strengthen collaboration to tackle drug abuse on campus
items.description: The Narcotics Control Commission (NACOC) has engaged the Management of the University of Ghana, Legon, to strengthen efforts to prevent substance abuse and drug-related activities among students. The engagement, led by NACOC Director-General, Major General Maxwell Obuba Mantey, focused on practical measures to curb the use, distribution and sale of illicit drugs on campus. A key concern raised was the reported sale of edible products laced with cannabis to unsuspecting students, particularly during hall week celebrations and other student-centred events. The discussions highlighted the need for closer cooperation between NACOC and the university to identify emerging patterns of drug use, strengthen preventive education and ensure students have access to counselling and other support services. Major General Mantey said the commission was concerned about the vulnerability of young people to substance abuse and its potential impact on their health, education, future careers and society. He stressed that NACOC’s mandate goes beyond enforcement and the arrest of persons involved in drug-related offences, noting that prevention, public education, counselling and rehabilitation were equally important. According to him, students already struggling with substance use should be encouraged to seek professional support rather than being left without assistance. Major General Mantey said NACOC was ready to work with the university to provide students with accurate information about the risks associated with substance abuse and encourage early intervention. He also stressed the need to address myths and misconceptions about cannabis and other substances, which he said could influence young people’s attitudes and behaviour. He said stronger collaboration between NACOC and educational institutions was necessary to protect students from exposure to drugs and maintain an environment conducive to learning and personal development. Director and Senior Counsellor of the University’s Careers and Counselling Directorate, Rev. Dr. Mrs. Bridget Ben-Naimah, welcomed the engagement and reaffirmed the University’s commitment to maintaining a drug-free campus. She outlined measures being used by the university to prevent and address drug-related activities, including counselling interventions and disciplinary procedures. Rev. Dr. Mrs. Ben-Naimah disclosed that students found to be involved in drug trafficking could face severe disciplinary action, including expulsion from the university and its halls of residence. She said the university would continue to take a firm stance against drug trafficking and other activities that threaten students’ well-being and the academic environment. She also stressed the importance of working with NACOC to complement the university’s internal measures with specialised expertise in drug prevention, education and enforcement. The engagement forms part of NACOC’s broader efforts to strengthen partnerships with educational institutions and prevent substance abuse among young people. Both institutions agreed on the need for sustained engagement, public education and early intervention to address drug-related challenges on campus. The collaboration is expected to strengthen preventive programmes, improve awareness among students and enhance support for those who may require counselling or other professional assistance. NACOC also urged students to be cautious about accepting food, sweets, drinks and other edible products from strangers, particularly during social events, and to report suspected drug-related activities to the appropriate authorities.

items.title: Boulkiemdé/Poa : Un étudiant consacre ses vacances aux travaux champêtres
items.description: BURKINA-BOULKIEMDE-POA-TAVAUX-CHAMPETRES Boulkiemdé/Poa : Un étudiant consacre ses vacances aux travaux champêtres Yaoguin, 27 août 2026 (AIB) – Étudiant en Lettres modernes à l’Université Norbert-Zongo de Koudougou, Bagué Souleymane met à profit ses vacances universitaires pour aider sa mère dans les travaux champêtres. Avec ses petits frères, il s’active notamment dans la culture du sorgho afin de contribuer aux besoins de la famille. « Pendant les vacances, je viens aider ma mère à cultiver afin que nous puissions subvenir à nos besoins grâce à la production du sorgho », a expliqué Bagué Souleymane. Selon lui, les travaux champêtres constituent une activité importante pour sa famille. Mais le démarrage effectif de la campagne agricole reste tributaire de la pluviométrie. « Nous attendons impatiemment la pluie pour pouvoir cultiver. Actuellement, la terre est sèche », a-t-il indiqué. Malgré les contraintes liées à la saison pluvieuse, le jeune étudiant entend consacrer une partie de ses vacances aux activités agricoles aux côtés des membres de sa famille. Cette implication traduit également la volonté de certains jeunes en milieu rural de concilier leurs études avec les activités agricoles, notamment pendant les vacances universitaires. Agence d'information du Burkina MK/PB/AS/ATA

items.title: It’s Bake Time
Yankhoba Diémé délivre le message du Président Faye aux dignitaires religieux et aux rois d’Oussouye
items.description: Ce jeudi 27 août 2026 à Oussouye, les tambours de la tradition ont résonné avec les voix de la République. Face aux rois, imams et responsables religieux, Yankhoba Diémé est venu porter le message de Bassirou Diomaye Faye, mais aussi plaider pour les prières nécessaires à la réalisation des grands projets promis à la Casamance. ZIGUINCHOR- Ce jeudi matin, la cour royale d’Oussouye s’est parée de son atmosphère solennelle. Dans ce haut lieu de la tradition diola, où la parole du roi conserve toute sa portée, le ministre des Forces armées, Yankhoba Diémé, est venu avec un message particulier : celui du chef de l’État. Devant Sa Majesté Maan Sibilumbaye Diédhiou, il a transmis les salutations de Bassirou Diomaye Faye et sollicité les prières du royaume pour accompagner les ambitions de transformation de la Casamance et du Sénégal. Au cœur des échanges, les infrastructures. Le deuxième pont de Ziguinchor, la route Ziguinchor-Cap Skirring, l’axe Oussouye-Mlomp, la liaison Bignona-Diouloulou-Kafountine ou encore le tronçon Ziguinchor-Mpack ont été évoqués par le ministre. « Le chef de l’État entend concrétiser l’ensemble de ces projets pour améliorer durablement le quotidien des populations casamançaises. Il viendra lui-même poser la première pierre du deuxième pont de Ziguinchor. La Casamance est au cœur de sa dynamique de transformation et il sollicite vos prières pour la réussite de ces chantiers », a déclaré Yankhoba Diémé. Du haut de son statut de gardien suprême de la tradition, le roi d’Oussouye a répondu par un message de reconnaissance et d’espérance. « Nous remercions profondément le président Bassirou Diomaye Faye. Dites-lui que nos prières l’accompagneront, lui-même et la Nation sénégalaise. Nous serons heureux et honorés de voir ces projets annoncés devenir une réalité », a assuré Maan Sibilumbaye Diédhiou. Tradition, foi et unité Après la cour royale, la délégation s’est rendue à la grande mosquée d’Oussouye pour un entretien avec l’imam ratib Souleymane Diané, avant de faire étape à la paroisse Sainte-Thérèse de l’Enfant-Jésus. Avec le Curé l’abbé Samson Delaka Kantoussan, responsable du dialogue interreligieux dans le clergé de Ziguinchor, les échanges ont porté sur la place de la foi dans la construction de la Nation. « La religion demeure l’un des socles essentiels de notre pays. Des institutions solides ont besoin d’un ancrage spirituel et moral fort. Nous sommes prêts à travailler dans la proximité et la collaboration, et nous apprécions vivement cette démarche du ministre », a souligné l’abbé Samson Kantoussan. Le périple s’est ensuite poursuivi à Kalobone, auprès du roi Koudiossobo Diatta, puis à Singhalène, dans la commune d’Oukout, où le ministre a rencontré les chefs coutumiers de Carounate, Djivente et Singhalène, organisateurs du « Bukut » 2026. Dans le royaume de Mlomp, Yankhoba Diémé a également rencontré le roi Sibilé Sambou. À chacun de ces gardiens de la tradition, il a transmis les salutations du chef de l’État et formulé le même vœu : la paix, la concorde et l’unité nationale. La tournée se poursuit dans la soirée avec l’évêque de Ziguinchor, Monseigneur Jean-Baptiste Valter Manga, avant une rencontre avec des responsables politiques de la région. Vendredi 28 août, le ministre mettra le cap sur le département de Bignona, où il rencontrera les imams ratibs et plusieurs autorités religieuses, avant de participer au Gamou des Chérifs à Kataba. Gaustin DIATTA (Correspondant)

items.title: NSMQ 2026: Presby SHS, Bompata dethrones OLAG to snatch seeded status, book quarter-final spot
items.description: Presby SHS, Bompata, has pulled off one of the biggest upsets of the 2026 National Science and Maths Quiz (NSMQ), knocking out seeded Our Lady of Grace Senior High School (OLAG) to advance to the quarter-finals. Bompata SHS held its nerve through a fiercely contested One-Eighth-stage encounter at the SMS Auditorium, finishing on 34 points to beat OLAG by six points. OLAG, the only private school to reach the semi-finals of the NSMQ last year, entered the contest as a seeded school and appeared poised to defend its status. But Presby SHS, Bompata, had other plans. The contest began with just one point separating the two sides. OLAG scored 17 points in Round One, narrowly ahead of Presby SHS, Bompata’s 16 points, while Kumasi Senior High Technical School managed 10. Presby SHS, Bompata, responded strongly in Round Two, taking the lead with 20 points as OLAG scored 16 and Kumasi Sec. Tech. added 13. The Problem of the Day offered little to separate the schools, with Presby SHS, Bompata, scoring 3 out of 10, while both OLAG and Kumasi Sec. Tech. managed 2 out of 10. Presby SHS, Bompata, extended its advantage in Round Three, posting 23 points against OLAG’s 18 and Kumasi Sec. Tech.’s 15. The contest then tightened in the subsequent round, with Presby SHS, Bompata, holding 28 points, while OLAG and Kumasi Sec. Tech. were tied at 22. With the quarter-final place within reach, Presby SHS, Bompata, kept its composure in the closing stages to finish on 34 points. OLAG could only manage 28 points, while Kumasi Sec. Tech. ended the contest on 22 points. The result means OLAG loses its seeded status, while Presby SHS, Bompata, seizes the seed. For OLAG, the defeat brings a stunning end to a campaign that began with the weight of being a seeded school and last year’s semi-final achievement. For Presby SHS, Bompata, however, the victory is a statement: the school has not only eliminated a seeded opponent but has also now inherited its place among the quarter-finalists. items.title: Les populations s’investissent dans la restauration de la mangrove
items.description: Les populations de Bouno veulent donner un nouveau souffle à la mangrove. Elles ont planté des propagules sur toute la rive du fleuve et bénéficié d’un offert un lot de matériel de nettoiement. SEDHIOU- Sur la rive du fleuve Casamance, dans le village de Bouno, les jeunes sont en premier ligne. Tenant chacun une plante à la main, ils poursuivent le reverdissement de la mangrove. Depuis deux ans, les associations comme green Sédhiou travaille avec les communautés pour lutter contre le changement climatique que subit Bouno et environ. « Nous avons acheté des camions de gravas que nous avons mis sur le long de la coté, afin d’atténuer l’avancée du fleuve Casamance. Mais ces solutions sont précaires, nous attendons encore l’appui des autorités pour vaincre le phénomène », plaide Ibou Dieye, président de l’association pour le développement durable de Bouno. Dans la région de Sédhiou, plusieurs localités côtières sont fragilisées par l’avancée des eaux. Nous avons constaté que la production agricole ne marche pas. Le reboisement est donc un espoir pour nous les femmes qui travaillons les rizières », assure Coumba Diop, présidente du groupement des femmes de Bouno. De son coté, Moussa Sadio estime que les mangroves sont très importantes alors que dans nos zones il y en a plus. Selon, ce membre des agents de protection des aires marines protégées, aujourd’hui, on ne peut plus parler de l’avancer de la mer sans parler de reboisement de la mangrove, c’est ce qui explique la mobilisation des populations, dit-il. Ce reboisement de Bounou intervient après celui de Dibanar et Djirédji. Le reboisement des mangroves est essentiel pour la sauvegarde de l’écosystème, notre venu à Bouno est donc important, reconnait Mariama Diakhaté, maire au conseil communal des enfants.« Nous avons aussi doté aux populations du matériel tel que des râteaux, des bennes à ordre, des pelles », dit-elle. Jonas Souloubany BASSENE (correspondant)

items.title: Nigeria’s economy stable, debt service declining – Oyedele
items.description: Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Mr Taiwo Oyedele, says Nigeria’s economy has stabilised. Oyedele started this on Thursday while briefing State House correspondents after the 158th meeting of the National Economic Council (NEC) in Abuja. He, however, said the priority was now to transform economic stability into shared prosperity for Nigerians. “Our real Gross Domestic Product growth rate was 3.89 per cent for Q1 of 2026, up from 3.13 per cent one year ago,” he said. Oyedele projected that Nigeria’s GDP growth rate would exceed four per cent in 2026, reflecting continued improvement in economic activity. He said inflation had also declined significantly, reaching 15.43 per cent at the end of July, compared with 24.94 per cent a year earlier. According to Oyedele, Nigeria’s trade surplus nearly doubled from N17.7 trillion in 2025 to N34.7 trillion by the first quarter of 2026. He said public debt remained moderate at 13.7 per cent of GDP, amounting to N159.28 trillion. “Debt service as a percentage of revenue is on the decline, from nearly 100 per cent as of 2022 to less than 60 per cent as of 2025,” he said. Oyedele said the economic progress was also reflected in improved assessments by international market rating agencies. “This is also part of the recognition by the market rating agencies,” he said. He said Fitch Ratings, Moody’s and S&P had all upgraded Nigeria’s sovereign credit rating between April 2025 and May 2026. “The first coordinated alignment in over a decade. So, they all agree,” Oyedele said. The minister said Nigeria also exited the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) grey list in October 2025. He added that the country exited the European Union’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing deficiency list in January 2026. According to him, the developments would reduce costs and friction associated with cross-border capital flows into Nigeria. Oyedele also announced Nigeria’s reclassification from an unclassified market to a frontier market. “Nigeria has now been reclassified to frontier market. This is good news for us as a country,” he said. He said the reclassification presented opportunities for Nigeria to accelerate economic growth and lift more citizens out of poverty. “We see opportunities ahead for the country, especially how we accelerate growth and lift our people out of poverty,” Oyedele said. He said NEC identified agriculture, energy, manufacturing, mining and the digital economy as priority sectors for accelerated development. Oyedele said 81.4 per cent of Nigerians worked in agriculture and non-tradable services, requiring greater attention to those sectors. “Council deliberated that there is a need for us to accelerate growth in these sectors where majority of our people work,” he said. He said stronger growth in those sectors would help reduce poverty and narrow the inequality gap across the country. “That way, we lift them out of poverty and we close the inequality gap,” Oyedele said. The minister, however, acknowledged that significant challenges remained and required coordinated efforts from the government and other stakeholders. “Key areas identified include geopolitical conflict, commodity shocks, persistent food inflation and the need to manage election cycle fiscal risk,” he said. Oyedele also highlighted the need to address negative pre-election narratives and ensure economic perceptions remained supported by available data. He said the government must focus on creating jobs while managing Nigeria’s vulnerability to foreign-exchange shocks. “There is a tendency to be negative pre-election, even though it is not supported by data, to ensure there is job-rich growth,” he said. He added that managing foreign-exchange vulnerability would remain essential to sustaining economic stability and translating current gains into broader prosperity. (NAN) The post Nigeria’s economy stable, debt service declining – Oyedele appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Immersion patriotique : Le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré appelle la jeunesse à faire du patriotisme un « combat de chaque instant »
items.description: À l’occasion de la clôture de la deuxième édition de l’Immersion patriotique obligatoire (IPO), le Président du Faso, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, a adressé un message solennel aux jeunes participants. Revenant sur les enseignements de cette expérience, le Chef de l'État les a invités à faire de l’humilité, de la solidarité, du courage, de la dignité et du patriotisme les piliers de leur engagement au service du Burkina Faso. C'est fini pour l'immersion patriotique 2026. 65 000 jeunes, bachelier session 2026, ont achevé leur formation sur la patriotisme, la discipline, l'amour de la Patrie et les idéaux de la Révolution progressiste populaire (RPP). Sans détour, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré a qualifié l’immersion patriotique de véritable « école de la vie ». Dormir à même le sol, partager les mêmes repas dans des conditions parfois rustiques, autant d’épreuves qui, selon lui, apprennent à dépasser les clivages sociaux. « Vous vous êtes retrouvés par-dessus toutes vos différences sociales », a souligné le chef de l'État, les exhortant à conserver cette humilité dans leur vie future. Le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré a ensuite plaidé pour un sursaut collectif. Le Burkina Faso, a-t-il rappelé, forme une communauté où chaque citoyen doit considérer l’autre comme un frère ou une sœur, sans égard à son origine, sa confession ou sa condition. Plutôt que de réclamer sans cesse des droits, les jeunes doivent, selon lui, interroger leur propre devoir. « Qu’est-ce que je peux faire pour mon voisin ? Pour mon quartier ? Pour ma commune ? Pour ma patrie ? », les a-t-il demandé de se questionner. L'immersion patriotique 2026 a pris fin Dans le contexte sécuritaire et social actuel, le Président du Faso a estimé que les Burkinabè ont « plus de devoirs que de droits », notamment dans la construction et la défense de la Nation. Il a particulièrement mis en garde les bacheliers et les futurs professionnels contre le découragement. Les conditions d’études restent imparfaites, a-t-il reconnu, malgré les efforts en matière d’infrastructures. L’Université constituera « un autre combat », a-t-il prévenu, appelant à un moral solide et à la persévérance. « Évitez les raccourcis », a-t-il martelé, estimant que la facilité mène à la compromission et à la perte des valeurs. Revenant sur les heures sombres de 2022, le Capitaine Traoré a vu dans le sens du devoir patriotique la raison qui a poussé certains militaires à assumer leurs responsabilités, malgré les risques. Une large part de son discours a été consacrée à la dignité et au refus de la trahison. Le « révolutionnaire burkinabè », a-t-il dit, doit se distinguer par son honnêteté et son rejet du mensonge. « Ne soyez pas des traîtres pour votre patrie. Travaillez, bossez dur, soyez des Burkinabè dignes », a lancé le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, avant de mettre en garde contre les manœuvres des puissances étrangères qui, selon lui, utilisent des relais locaux avant de les abandonner. Enfin, le chef de l’État a exhorté la jeunesse à prendre pleinement conscience de sa responsabilité dans le développement national. « Personne, je dis bien personne, ne viendra développer cette patrie pour nous », a déclaré Ibrahim Traoré, rappelant que chaque État défend d’abord ses propres intérêts. La terre héritée des ancêtres, a-t-il ajouté, est un patrimoine à préserver et à transmettre. 65 000 jeunes ont pris part à l'immersion patriotique À travers l’IPO, le Burkina Faso entend former un citoyen plus conscient de ses devoirs envers la collectivité. La deuxième promotion rejoindra donc les Universités et la vie active avec cette expérience en mémoire. Le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré a annoncé la création de centres nationaux d’immersion, ouverts à d’autres Burkinabè, sur une base volontaire ou obligatoire. Enfin, le Président du Faso a souhaité aux jeunes une bonne rentrée académique et une heureuse insertion professionnelle. Lire aussi : Immersion patriotique 2026 : « La jeunesse ne doit pas être un simple témoin de l’histoire, elle doit en être un acteur engagé » (Porte-parole des appelés à l’immersion) Jean-François SOMÉ et Oumarou KONATÉ Minute.bf

items.title: Senyo Hosi calls for policy certainty, productive infrastructure and stronger human capital to transform Africa
items.description: Founder and Executive Chairman of Kleeve and Tove Ltd, Senyo Hosi, has called for closer cooperation between capable governments and competitive businesses to drive Africa’s economic transformation. Mr Hosi said African countries needed governments that could provide clear rules, invest in public goods and create an environment in which businesses could create value and jobs. He made the remarks at the Students & Young Professionals Africa Liberty Academy (SYPALA) 2026 at the University of Professional Studies, Accra (UPSA), organised by IMANI Africa on Thursday, August 27. Speaking on the topic, “Beyond Politics: How Business and Public Policy Can Drive Africa’s Transformation,” Mr Hosi said Africa’s development would depend on how effectively governments, businesses and citizens worked together. “Africa absolutely needs capable states and competitive markets working together,” he said. “Government setting clear rules and investing in public goods. Business creating value when jobs and citizens holding both are comfortable.” According to him, five key drivers must be addressed if African countries are to achieve sustainable economic growth and create meaningful opportunities for their growing populations. Mr Hosi identified policy certainty and the rule of law as the first major driver of development, arguing that investors were more willing to commit their resources when institutions were reliable. “Capital is patient where rules are credible,” he said. “Entrepreneurs invest where contracts are enforced. Property is protected and regulations do not change overnight,” he added. Mr Hosi said African countries needed to strengthen institutions in ways that would reduce excessive discretion and increase public confidence. “Africa must build institutions that reduce discretion and increase trust,” he said. He said that predictable policies were essential for encouraging long-term investment and giving entrepreneurs the confidence to build businesses that could survive beyond changes in political administrations. Mr Hosi also highlighted productive infrastructure as a critical requirement for economic competitiveness. He listed roads, ports, railways, electricity, broadband, water systems and logistics as important platforms for production and trade. “Every production you are running in your country is in competition with another production that has access to your country,” he said. He warned that high energy costs and poor infrastructure could make businesses in African countries uncompetitive. “So when you are paying for electricity at a higher rate because your government has negotiated reckless IPP contracts, what you are going to do is become uncompetitive as production is concerned,” he said. Mr Hosi said that infrastructure decisions had direct consequences for businesses, workers and consumers. “The lights can be gone, but it will never make sense to create employment for you,” he said. He pointed to the African Development Bank’s assessment that closing Africa’s infrastructure gap could increase GDP growth by an estimated two percentage points a year. For Mr Hosi, infrastructure planning must go beyond simply building physical assets and should instead focus on their contribution to productivity, jobs, value chains and markets. “Infrastructure must therefore be planned around productivity, value chains, jobs, and markets,” he said. He also highlighted the economic cost of poor transport systems, noting that long travel times reduced productivity and increased fuel costs. “You see that unproductive time you spend on that road? It’s a very pathetic story,” he said, comparing travel times in Africa with those in the United States. Mr Hosi said that public policy decisions could not be considered in isolation because each decision could have wider economic consequences. “Every single decision has consequences,” he said. “Every decision within the public policy sphere has consequences.” The third driver, according to Mr Hosi, is human capital for a changing economy. He said Africa’s young population could become a major economic advantage, but only if young people were equipped with the skills, values and opportunities needed to participate productively in the economy. “Africa’s youth advantage becomes a demographic dividend only when we match these gifts with skills, health, discipline, ethics, and opportunity,” he said. Mr Hosi placed emphasis on ethics, saying weak ethical standards had become a serious challenge for businesses and public institutions. “I will drive and drive in on ethics. We have a highly less ethical youth today,” he said. He acknowledged that older generations also had a responsibility to examine the example they had set for young people. “Because to be fair to you, we have been less of a good example,” he said. Using an experience from Canada, Mr Hosi illustrated how trust and personal responsibility could reduce the cost of doing business. He recalled visiting a farm where customers could take vegetables from a shed and leave their payments in a container without direct supervision. “Do you know what the farmer has done? He has taken out an operating cost,” he said, arguing that trust reduced the need for additional controls and monitoring. Mr Hosi contrasted that experience with what he described as the challenges faced by businesses in Africa. “In Africa, when you run a business, you must budget for staff debt. You must budget for staff debt,” he said. He also urged young people to rethink their attitudes towards wealth and status, particularly the pressure to acquire material possessions immediately after leaving university. “Every one of you comes out of school, and you’re in a hurry to own a car. Everybody wants to impress somebody,” he said. “But that is not a natural progression of life. It takes time.” While acknowledging the ambition of young people, Mr Hosi said that energy needed to be directed towards productive activities rather than shortcuts. “I like that energy, but we apply that very wrongly,” he said. He warned that the weakening of ethical standards affected society at every level, from politics and business to workplaces and partnerships. “Our value systems are broken down. Our politicians are in disaster. Our businessmen, we are disasters,” he said. “The politicians don’t do it alone, they do it with us.” Mr Hosi said improving human capital also required a major rethink of education. “Our education system must also connect with industry,” he said, calling for technical, vocational, digital, financial and entrepreneurial skills to become mainstream. He identified critical thinking, innovation and creativity as particularly important skills for young people. “At the heart of it, for me, is critical thinking. Innovation, creativity. A lot of it is really lost in today’s education,” he said. Mr Hosi identified deeper local capital and domestic resource mobilisation as another important driver of transformation. He said Africa could not rely solely on foreign aid and external borrowing to finance development. “Africa can absolutely not finance transformation only through aid and external borrowing,” he said. He referred to African Development Bank analysis suggesting that the continent could mobilise about $1.43 trillion in additional domestic resources through reforms in fiscal systems, natural resource governance, finance, business and human capital. However, Mr Hosi said governments would only be able to mobilise greater domestic resources if citizens trusted them to use public funds responsibly. “But people will trust the state with more resources only when spending is transparent and accountable,” he said. He therefore called for stronger accountability and a change in the values of the people entrusted with public resources. “We need to change our value systems and the kind of people we put out there,” he said. Mr Hosi said the ultimate objective should be to create and sustain jobs while improving the quality of life of citizens. “To do that transformation, we need to sustain the jobs and the meaningful lives that you need. You can’t be passive about that,” he told the young audience. The fifth driver he identified was regional integration and value addition. Mr Hosi encouraged young Africans to look beyond their individual countries and consider the opportunities presented by the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA). He said the agreement connected a potential market of about 1.3 billion people across 55 countries, with a combined GDP of about $3.1 trillion. “As a young person, you should start thinking about that opportunity,” he said. He cited World Bank analysis estimating that deeper implementation of the AfCFTA could create almost 18 million additional jobs by 2035. “That gives you a pathway,” he said. However, Mr Hosi said that the potential of regional integration would not be realised automatically. He said it would require reforms in customs, standards, trade, transportation, infrastructure and finance, alongside stronger and more competitive African businesses. “When you see your politicians and policymakers, you ask them, how are they leveraging this to create a better opportunity and a better future for you?” he said. He said that policymakers must create the right conditions, businesses must invest and create value, and citizens, particularly young people, must demand accountability and contribute to building stronger institutions. He identified policy certainty and the rule of law, productive infrastructure, human capital for a changing economy, deeper local capital and domestic resource mobilisation, and regional integration and value addition as essential to Africa’s transformation. He urged young people to take an active interest in how public policy and business decisions shape their future. “You guys have the consequences of our actions. And that’s why you must hold us back up,” he said. “That’s why your orientation must change.”
